body_markdown:
Bring in a delivery partner on a grid or network modernization program and the first few weeks rarely go on delivery. They go on discovery. Which sites are in scope, what’s actually on them, who holds the lease, which version of the record is right, and who can say so with authority.


That work has to happen. It just doesn’t have to happen on the partner’s clock, at the partner’s rate, with the program waiting. Most of it can be done before anyone arrives, and the customers who get the most from a partner are usually the ones who did it first.


Here’s what a delivery partner needs from you before day one.


### A baseline you can name, even if it isn’t clean


Nobody expects a perfect record on day one. What a partner needs is a baseline that’s honestly described: which four sources hold the picture (leasing and commercial, network, field and ops, permitting), which one governs which fact, and a written list of the gaps you already know about.


That list matters more than it sounds. A partner handed a known list of discrepancies starts resolving them. A partner handed a record presented as clean spends the first weeks finding out it isn’t, and the program learns it from a delay instead of a document.


### One person who owns the record


Somebody on your side has to be accountable for the estate record itself, with the authority to decide when two sources disagree. Leasing owns the lease, network owns the equipment, ops own the work order. Nobody owns the picture that joins them, which is why a partner so often ends up asking the same question of three teams and getting three answers.


You don’t need a new department. You need a named person who can say “this source wins for this fact” and have it stick. Without that, every conflict the partner surfaces waits for a meeting.


### Access to the sources, and the people who understand them


Exports and read access to the four systems get a partner started. The person who knows why a particular field is unreliable gets them moving. Every estate has quirks: the status code that means something different in one region, the spreadsheet everyone trusts more than the system, the site that was decommissioned informally.


Line up access before day one, and name one person per source who can explain it. Access without context produces a tidy-looking reconciliation that’s wrong in ways only your people would have spotted.


### A view of progress that doesn’t run through one person


On most programs, the program manager is the integration layer, carrying status between systems by hand. A delivery partner who joins that arrangement doesn’t fix it. They become a second person doing the same manual stitching, and the program gets one more single point of failure.


Before day one, decide where progress will live so that crews, partner and program office all read from the same place. If completed work only becomes visible when someone logs it, the partner will be planning against a picture that’s weeks old, the same as everyone else.


### Agreed expectations for the people outside your systems


EPCs, attachers and landowners won’t adopt your tools, and a delivery partner can’t make them. What can be settled early is how they report: what they confirm, how often, and in what form. If real status lives in an inbox, the partner inherits the inbox.


This is far easier to agree at the start of an engagement than to retrofit once crews are mobilized and every update is already arriving by email.


### A plan for field verification


A reconciled desk record is still a set of claims about the physical world. Decide up front how much gets verified in the field, by whom, and in what order. The sequence matters: consolidate the sources first, then verify what’s left. Send technicians out against a single partial record and information held in the other sources goes unchecked, and can be overwritten the next time that record is updated.


Settle the sample size and the access arrangements before day one, and field verification becomes a scheduled step instead of a negotiation.


### Procurement and security decisions made early


Onboarding a new vendor often means procurement, contracting and security review, and those can take longer than the work they sit in front of. A partner can be ready to start while the tooling they need is still waiting on paperwork.


This is one reason the[West Monroe and Sitenna team-up](https://sitenna.com/west-monroe-and-sitenna-announce-team-up-to-help-utilities-modernize-their-infrastructure/) was built the way it was. West Monroe can introduce Sitenna into its existing engagements, so utilities don’t have to contract with and onboard a separate vendor first. The time to value shortens, and the benefits can show up in weeks, sometimes days.


### Why this list is worth the effort


Every item above is cheaper to settle before day one than after. A gap found at kick-off is a correction. The same gap found after crews are scheduled is a re-plan and found at handover it’s a missed commitment. The error is identical in each case. What it costs to fix multiplies at every stage it survives.


A delivery partner with a named baseline, an owner, access, a shared view of progress, agreed reporting rules, a verification plan and clear procurement can spend their first weeks building. Without them, they spend those weeks discovering.
